profile.summary: Luke presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and the Savior of universal reach: coming as the Son of God and descendant of David, he announces and incarnates the good news for Jews and Gentiles, poor and rich, men and women, close and marginalized. The gospel highlights its compassion for the lost, its authority in teaching, healing and liberation, the opposition of the religious leaders, the deliberate ascent to Jerusalem to suffer, die innocent and rise, and the continuity of mission by the Spirit to all the nations.
profile.setting: The book was written amid the growing conflict between the church and the synagogue in the second half of the first century. The Christian community still saw itself as fulfillment of Israel, not as a new religion; therefore, Luke insists that the promises of the Scriptures are fulfilled in Jesus and continue to be fulfilled in the mission of the church. There is uncertainty about the place of writing: Rome, Ephesus, Caesarea and Achaea have already been suggested. Also the date is debated: some defend about 59-63 AD, others place the work between 70-90 AD. The nominal recipient is Theophilus, probably a patron and/or believer who needed confirmation of the faith, but the work clearly also targets a wider Christian audience, largely Gentile.

structure.label: Prologue and the birth of Jesus
structure.description: Formal introduction of the work and accounts of the birth and childhood of Jesus, emphasizing the Jewish roots of salvation and the fulfillment of promises.

structure.label: Preparation and beginning of ministry
structure.description: John the Baptist, the baptism, the temptation and the beginning of the public ministry of Jesus, with the proclamation of the Kingdom and first resistance in Nazareth.

structure.label: Ministry in Galilee
structure.description: Teaching with authority, healing, expulsion of demons, called disciples and the summit in Peter's confession, followed by the proclamation of suffering and death in Jerusalem.

structure.label: Way to Jerusalem
structure.description: The long travel section brings together remarkable teachings and parables, showing God's mercy to lost, poor, sinners, Samaritans, women and Gentiles.

structure.label: Final confrontation, passion and cross
structure.description: In Jerusalem, Jesus faces opposition, announces judgment, is imprisoned, judged, and crucified as just suffering; his innocence is underlined in the narrative of passion.

structure.label: Resurrection and shipping
structure.description: The resurrection, the way to Emmaus and the ascension show that the death of Jesus fulfilled the Scriptures and opened the global mission of the people of God.

themes: Jesus as promised Messiah and Davidic King
Salvation for all peoples, including those outside Israel
Mercy of God for the lost, poor and sinners
Innocence and voluntary suffering of Jesus on the cross
Fulfillment of Scripture and continuity of mission by the Spirit
readingKeys: Notice how Luke links promise and fulfillment, especially when it shows that the story of Jesus was already in advance in the Scriptures.
Pay attention along the way to Jerusalem: in it, Luke gathers parables and encounters that highlight who enters the Kingdom and who rejects it.
Note the social and religious contrasts - rich and poor, Pharisees and sinners, Jews and Gentiles, men and women - to perceive how the gospel redefines who belongs to God's people.
profile.cautions: The traditional authorship attributes the work to Luke, Paul's companion and physician, but the book itself is anonymous; identification depends on tradition and internal evidence, not of explicit signature. There is also debate about date and place of composition, so it is appropriate to treat them as plausible hypotheses, not as certainties. The reading should consider Lucas along with Atos, because the two volumes form a literary and theological unit.

dossier.narratedEra: Luke's narrative takes place in the Ith-century Judaism, under Herod, under Roman rule, with the ministry of John the Baptist, Jesus in Galilee, the ascent to Jerusalem, the crucifixion, the resurrection and the ascension. The notes place some episodes in concrete milestones of the period, such as the functioning Temple, the synagogue practice, the rural world of Galilee and Jerusalem of Easter time.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is situated by the introductory note in the middle of the late 1st century AD, in context of the growth of the conflict between church and synagogue. There are two main proposals: oldest date, about 59-63 AD, linked to the end of Acts with Paul imprisoned in Rome; or later date, about 70-90 AD, especially if Luke used Mark, written in the late 1960s and around the Jewish war of 66-70. The author is traditionally identified as Luke, Paul's doctor and companion, although the gospels are technically anonymous.

politics.title: Herod and Judea under local government subordinate to Rome
politics.detail: At the beginning of the gospel, the birth of John the Baptist is dated to the reign of Herod, king of Judea, which places the narrative within a Jewish political scene administered under imperial influence.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the first chapters as a situated story, not as an abstract account; it also reinforces Luke's care to anchor the gospel in real rulers.

politics.title: Roman Empire and threat of public punishment
politics.detail: Luke 24 notes that the Romans performed crucifixions in public and strategic places to serve as an example and contain revolts; this illuminates the scandal of the cross and the astonishment of the disciples on the way to Emmaus.
politics.readingImpact: The crucifixion of Jesus appears not only as religious suffering, but also as exemplary political punishment of the empire.

politics.title: Religious Authorities and Opposition to Jesus" Ministry
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction highlights that religious leaders opposed Jesus, and that the conflict between church and synagogue was already intensified in the period of composition.
politics.readingImpact: The reader must realize that Jesus" rejection in Luke is not a peripheral detail, but an interpretative axis of the plot and the context of reception.

politics.title: Division between Jews Who Reject and Jews Who Reject Jesus
politics.detail: The introductory note states that many Jews rejected the good news while Gentiles entered the church; the central question became who are the true people of God.
politics.readingImpact: This affects the reading of rejection episodes in Nazareth, Jerusalem, and other contexts, showing them as part of a larger identity dispute.

politics.title: Trial on Jerusalem and continuity in Acts
politics.detail: The introduction links Jerusalem's rejection of divine judgment and the continuity of that pattern in Acts.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is led to see passion not only as a biographical end, but as part of a history of prophetic rejection and missionary transition.

customs.title: Marriage arranged and engagement as legal contract
customs.detail: In Luke 1, Joseph and Mary are in formal engagement, and the note describes the Jewish engagement as a legal contract between families; girls usually married in adolescence.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to understand the social and legal seriousness of the announcement to Mary, as well as the public vulnerability of Jesus" family.

customs.title: Sterility as social shame
customs.detail: Isabella's infertility is explained as a reason for stigma and shame, because motherhood was seen as the greatest female vocation in the culture described by the note.
customs.readingImpact: John's birth appears as a reversal of shame and divine intervention, and not just as a biological miracle.

customs.title: Priesthood, order and service in the Temple
customs.detail: The note explains that there were twenty-four priestly orders and that the service in the sanctuary was decided by lot; the priest could receive such privilege rarely in life. It also distinguishes the building of the Temple (naos) from the atriums (hieron).
customs.readingImpact: This broadens the solemnity of the scene of Zechariah: the angelic announcement occurs at the most sacred moment of a priest's life, in the heart of the Israelite cult.

customs.title: Circumcision to the eighth day and incorporation into the pact
customs.detail: In John's circumcision, the note recalls the ordinance of circumcision on the eighth day and its meaning as the child's insertion into the community of the covenant. He also mentions the custom of naming the child with the name of a relative, which explains the surprise of the family when he receives the name "João."
customs.readingImpact: The reading highlights that John is already born marked by a pactual belonging and by a name of divine initiative, not of family tradition.

customs.title: Hospitality and shared meal
customs.detail: On the way to Emmaus, the hospitality of the Middle East required to offer food and shelter to the traveler; the meal becomes the moment of recognition of the resurrected Jesus.
customs.readingImpact: The scene transforms a daily custom into a theological sign: the table reveals the identity of the Risen One and symbolizes the Messianic banquet.

customs.title: Crucifixion as public warning and debt arrest
customs.detail: The note in Luke 24 notes the Roman use of crucifixion as a public example; in Luke 12, the parable of reconciliation before the court presupposes litigation for debt and possible imprisonment of the debtor.
customs.readingImpact: The legal and punitive world of the 1st century reinforces the burden of Jesus" warnings about judgment and urgency of success.

language.title: Prologue in Greek formal and historiographical
language.detail: Luke 1:1-4 is described as formal prologue, in the style of the best Greek writers of the time, with high-level literary Greek and explicit historiographical purpose.
language.readingImpact: The gospel should be read as carefully investigated and literariously elaborated narrative, not as a loose collection of traditions.

language.title: "Cumprido" as fulfillment of the promises of the Old Testament
language.detail: The note says that the term may mean simply "realized," but in Luke points to the fulfillment of the promises of the Old Testament, especially those concerning Jesus.
language.readingImpact: The language of fulfillment anchors Luke's reading in the continuity between the Scriptures of Israel and the gospel.

language.title: The structure of songs: Magnificat and Benedictus
language.detail: The notes identify Mary's song as Magnificat and that of Zechariah as Benedictus, both with strong biblical resonance and thematic of reversal and salvation.
language.readingImpact: The beginning of the gospel already interprets the story of Jesus through prophetic praise, highlighting social reversal, mercy and covenant.

language.title: "Pobre," "pecador" and "lost" as recurrent theological categories
language.detail: The notes emphasize that Luke presents salvation to the poor, sinners, excluded and lost; the formula of 19:10 summarizes the mission of Jesus.
language.readingImpact: The vocabulary directs reading to God's active mercy and for the inclusion of marginalized, not for social merit.

language.title: Image of yeast and hypocrisy
language.detail: In Luke 12, leaven symbolizes the penetrating power of sin, and Pharisaic hypocrisy is described as something that spreads throughout the mass.
language.readingImpact: The image teaches that false religious attitudes have a diffuser effect; the problem is not only individual, but community.

language.title: Divine liabilities and revelation
language.detail: In Luke 24, expressions such as "were prevented from recognizing" and "sus eyes have been opened" are explained as divine passives, suggesting God's action behind the scene.
language.readingImpact: Reading makes it more evident that the recognition of the Risen One is a gift revealed by God, not mere psychological chance.

timeline.title: Reign of Herod at the birth of John the Baptist
timeline.detail: The initial narrative is anchored in the reign of Herod, King of Judea, placing the beginning of the gospel at the end of the Herodian era.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology shows that Luke wants to link the beginning of salvation to a concrete moment in Jewish history under local and Roman rule.

timeline.title: Ministry of John as forerunner of Elias
timeline.detail: The notes link John to the prophetic expectation of Malachi and the role of precursor before the time of salvation.
timeline.readingImpact: The appearance of John is not isolated, but a milestone of transition between promise and fulfillment.

timeline.title: First day of the week and early Christian worship
timeline.detail: The resurrection is situated very early on Sunday, and the note states that the early church began to worship on the first day of the week because of the resurrection.
timeline.readingImpact: This clarifies why the Easter morning has foundational weight for Christian practice, without confusing it with the Jewish Sabbath.

timeline.title: Third day after crucifixion
timeline.detail: The note says that Jesus resurrected on the third day counting Friday as the first and Sunday as the third.
timeline.readingImpact: The formulation helps to read the chronology of passion and resurrection according to the old mode of inclusive counting.

timeline.title: Passion, Emmaus and recognition at the table
timeline.detail: The account of Emmaus is presented as Luke's unique contribution, linked to the scrituristic interpretation of the cross and the revelation of the Risen One in the fraction of the bread.
timeline.readingImpact: The sequence shows that the resurrection is read in the light of Scripture and the table, not as a loose event.

timeline.title: Ascension as exaltation and beginning of mission
timeline.detail: Luke 24 ends with the ascension, also described in Acts, and the note states that it confirms the vindication, exaltation, and enthronement of Jesus; the Spirit is promised for the future mission.
timeline.readingImpact: Lucas's ending does not end the story, but projects it to continue in Acts and the mission to the Gentiles.

investigation: The traditional authorship associates the gospel with Luke, Paul's doctor and companion; Matthew Henry's note also features diverse ancient traditions, but considers them uncertain in some points.
The notes agree that Luke and Acts form a literary and theological unity; the date of composition remains debated between an older date and a later date.
There is a strong emphasis on the Old Testament promises fulfilled in Jesus, but the notes use this as internal theological reading, not as independent historical proof.
The material on the conflict between church and synagogue is an interpretative frame of introductory notes; he explains Luke's emphasis on many rejection in Israel and the Gentile mission.
Observations about women, poor, Samaritans, sinners and Gentiles reflect the focus of the commentary, but not all gospel episodes receive equal attention in the attached notes.
Some ancient traditions mentioned by Matthew Henry as Luke being one of the seventy disciples or even a painter appear as conjectures and not as firm assertions.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the provided notes and is therefore selective. The cover is richer in Luke 1, 12, and 24, because they were the sections attached; there are no specific notes of many central chapters of the gospel. The statements about date, place of writing and authorship are presented as proposals of the sources, without an attempt to resolve disputes with external knowledge. Nor do we expand unexplained themes, such as details of the Roman provincial administration, exact chronologies of Jesus' life or general Jewish customs, when they do not appear in the notes. Where the source offers more than one possibility, as on the date of composition or in some ancient traditions about Luke, this was maintained as debate and not as certainty.
